title: House Buttermilk Biscuits
dek: The counter biscuit: fat to flour at 1:2.8, cut tall, baked hot, no twisting the cutter.
intro: Everything about a biscuit is decided in the first five minutes, before it goes anywhere near heat. Cold fat left in visible pieces makes steam pockets and steam pockets make layers; fat that has melted into the flour makes a scone-ish crumb that is fine but is not this. The ratio here is one part butter to two point eight parts flour by weight. At 1:2 you get something closer to pastry, rich and short and inclined to go greasy at the base. At 1:4 you get a bread roll. This sits where a biscuit should: tall, flaky, and structurally sound enough to hold an egg.

items: 480 g all-purpose flour, or soft winter wheat flour (about 4 cups)
170 g cold unsalted butter, cut in 1 cm cubes (about 12 tbsp)
20 g melted butter for the tops (about 1 1/2 tbsp)

method: Put the cubed butter in the freezer for 10 minutes and heat the oven to 450°F (230°C). A hot oven is half of the lift: the steam has to fire before the fat has time to melt out.
Whisk the flour, baking powder, soda, salt and sugar together thoroughly. Under-mixed leavening gives you one bitter biscuit and eight flat ones.

Cut in the butter with your fingertips or a pastry blender until the largest pieces are the size of a hazelnut and the rest is coarse and irregular. Stop while you can still see butter. If it looks like even sand, it has gone too far.

Pour in the buttermilk all at once and stir with a fork until it just comes together in a shaggy mass with a few dry patches. Twelve or fifteen strokes, not thirty. Hydration here is 71% on the flour, which feels wetter than most people expect.

Tip it onto a floured counter, pat into a rectangle about 2 cm thick, and fold it in thirds like a letter. Turn it 90 degrees and repeat twice more. That is three folds and it is where the layers come from.

Pat out to a final 2.5 cm thick. Flour a 2 3/4 inch cutter and press straight down without twisting — twisting seals the cut edge and the biscuit rises lopsided or not at all. Push straight down, lift straight up.
Set them on a tray so the sides touch. Biscuits climbing on each other rise higher than biscuits standing alone; the touching edges stay soft and give the dough something to hold onto.
Brush the tops with melted butter, avoiding the cut sides, and scatter a little flaky salt.

Bake 14 to 18 minutes, until the tops are deep gold, the sides show dry flaky seams rather than a wet-looking band, and the biscuits feel light when lifted. An instant-read through the side reads 205°F (96°C).

Eat them within the hour. If they came out short and dense, the likely culprits in order are: warm butter, over-mixing, a twisted cutter, or leavening past its date of usefulness — test it by dropping a teaspoon in hot water and watching whether it fizzes hard.
notes: Soft winter wheat flour, low protein, makes a more tender biscuit. All-purpose works; bread flour makes them chewy.
Grating frozen butter on the coarse side of a box grater is faster than cutting it in and keeps the pieces colder.
Scraps re-patted make a fine biscuit and an ugly one. Do not re-roll more than once.
storage: Same day. Day two they are for splitting, toasting hard under a grill, and covering in something.

title: When There Is No Buttermilk
dek: Three substitutions that actually work, with the liquid adjusted for each, plus the biscuit to test them on.
intro: Buttermilk is doing two separate jobs. It is acidic, which reacts with baking soda for lift and tenderises gluten so the crumb stays short. It is also thick, because culturing thickens milk, and that viscosity is why a buttermilk dough hydrates without going slack. Most substitutes replace the acid and forget the body, which is why milk soured with vinegar makes a wetter, flatter biscuit if you use it gram for gram. Here are the three worth knowing, corrected for that, and a plain biscuit to try them in.

ingredients.group: Pick one substitute for 280 g buttermilk
items: Soured milk: 260 g whole milk plus 15 g lemon juice or white vinegar, stood 10 minutes
Thinned yogurt: 200 g plain whole-milk yogurt plus 80 g milk, whisked smooth
Powdered: 25 g cultured buttermilk powder whisked into the dry flour, plus 280 g water
140 g cold unsalted butter, cubed (about 10 tbsp)
280 g of your chosen substitute, cold

method: If you are souring milk, stir the acid in and leave it 10 minutes. It will look curdled and slightly thickened. That is the acid doing its part; it will never reach the body of real buttermilk, which is why the milk here is measured at 260 g rather than 280 and the acid makes up the rest. Swap it gram for gram and the dough runs wet.
If you are thinning yogurt, whisk until there are no lumps at all. Lumps of yogurt do not disperse in a barely-mixed dough and each one bakes into a pale wet spot.
Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) and whisk the flour, baking powder, soda and salt together — plus the buttermilk powder if you are using that route.

Cut in the cold butter until the biggest pieces are hazelnut sized and the mixture is coarse and uneven. This is a 1:2.9 fat to flour dough, near enough the same as the house biscuit, so the substitutes are being tested rather than the ratio.

Add the liquid all at once and stir with a fork until it just holds together. If it is drier than you expect, add another 15 g rather than working it harder. Yogurt doughs usually want a splash more; soured milk almost never does.
Pat out 2 cm thick, fold in thirds twice, then pat to 2.5 cm.
Cut with a floured 2 3/4 inch cutter, pressing straight down, and set them on a tray with the sides touching.
Bake 14 to 17 minutes, until risen and deep gold on top with dry seams down the sides, and an instant-read reads 205°F (96°C).

Judge them honestly. Yogurt gives the closest result and the softest crumb. Soured milk gives good lift and a slightly thinner flavour. Powder is the best of the three for keeping in a cupboard and the one worth having when the road is closed and the shop is shut.
What does not work: sour cream straight, which is too fat and too thick and bakes greasy; and lemon juice in cream, which curdles into something you cannot mix in evenly.
notes: Plain kefir is an excellent swap at a straight one-to-one and needs no adjustment at all.
If you are out of both buttermilk and acid, drop the baking soda and use 18 g of baking powder with plain milk. It will be milder and a shade less tender.
storage: Cultured buttermilk powder keeps for a year in a cool cupboard, which is why it is on the shelf here.

title: Laminated Flaky Biscuits
dek: Frozen grated butter, six folds, and a biscuit that peels apart in sheets.
totalTime: 1 hour 30 minutes, with two chilling rests
intro: This is the biscuit for people who want to count the layers. The fat runs at one to two and a half, richer than the everyday version, and the dough is folded six times with chilling in between, which is proper lamination rather than a nod at it. The result peels apart in sheets like a rough puff pastry that has decided to be a biscuit. The cost is time and a colder kitchen than you probably have — if the butter warms and smears, you lose the layers and end up with something merely good.

items: 200 g unsalted butter, frozen solid (about 14 tbsp)

method: Freeze the butter for at least an hour, wrapped. Whisk the dry ingredients together in a wide bowl and put the bowl in the fridge while you wait.
Grate the frozen butter on the coarse side of a box grater directly into the cold flour, stopping twice to toss the shreds through so they stay separate. Work fast; the butter needs to stay frozen.
Add the buttermilk and stir with a fork until it forms a shaggy, barely-together dough. Hydration is 64%, lower than the everyday biscuit because there is more fat carrying the moisture.
Tip onto a floured counter and pat into a 20 by 30 cm rectangle. Fold in thirds, turn 90 degrees, pat out and fold again. Two folds, then wrap it and refrigerate 20 minutes.

Repeat: two more folds, another 20 minutes in the fridge, then two final folds. Six in total. If at any point the butter starts to look shiny or smeared rather than marbled, stop and chill it immediately — that is the failure this recipe is built to avoid.
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). This one bakes slightly cooler than a plain biscuit so the interior sets before the outside darkens.
Pat the dough to 3 cm thick. Cut with a floured 2 3/4 inch cutter, straight down, no twist. Or square the dough off with a knife and cut nine rectangles, which wastes nothing and rises just as well.
Arrange on a parchment-lined tray with the sides touching, brush the tops with melted butter, and freeze the whole tray for 10 minutes before it goes in the oven.

Bake 20 to 24 minutes, until the biscuits have climbed and separated into visible leaves at the sides, the tops are deep gold, and an instant-read reads 205°F (96°C). They should feel hollow-light for their size.
Scatter flaky salt over the hot tops. Let them stand five minutes; the layers set as they cool slightly and they tear more cleanly.
If they leaned or spilled sideways, the folds were uneven or the cutter dragged. If they were tall but not flaky, the butter melted somewhere along the way.
notes: A cold room is an ingredient. In a warm kitchen, chill between every single fold rather than every second one.
European-style butter at 82% fat has less water and laminates better, though it also browns faster.
storage: Same day for the layers. They freeze well unbaked — cut, freeze solid, and bake from frozen with five minutes added.

title: Drop Biscuits
dek: No cutter, no folding, no counter. Twenty-five minutes from cupboard to table.
intro: A drop biscuit is a wetter dough spooned straight onto a tray, and it trades layers for speed and a craggy top that catches butter. Because there is no rolling, there is no gluten development to worry about and no reason to keep the fat in pieces, so this version uses melted butter, which makes it a one-bowl job with a fork. It is the thing to make when soup is nearly ready and there is no bread in the house, which on a wet evening is most evenings.

items: 115 g unsalted butter, melted and cooled slightly (about 8 tbsp)
A pinch of flaky salt, or 1 tsp cracked black pepper

method: Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) and line a tray with parchment.
Whisk the dry ingredients together in a large bowl.

Stir the melted butter into the cold buttermilk. It will seize into small lumps and clumps almost immediately. That is what you want — those lumps are pieces of butter and they behave like cut-in butter once they hit the flour.

Pour the buttermilk mixture into the flour and stir with a fork until just combined, about ten strokes. The dough should be wet and rough, close to 93% hydration, and it should hold its shape on a spoon.
Drop heaped tablespoons, about 70 g each, onto the tray, leaving four centimetres between them. Do not smooth them; the rough peaks brown and crisp and that is the appeal.
Brush the tops with melted butter and season.
Bake 12 to 16 minutes, until the peaks are well browned, the bases are golden when you lift one with a spatula, and an instant-read reads 205°F (96°C).
Serve hot. These stale faster than a cut biscuit because of the larger surface area, so time them to come out when the food does.
If they spread into flat pancakes, the butter was too hot when it met the buttermilk and dissolved into it instead of clumping, or the dough sat too long before baking.
notes: Add 100 g grated sharp cheddar and a teaspoon of garlic powder for the version that goes with chowder.
The dough does not keep. Mix it when the oven is already hot.
storage: Eat them the same hour. They reheat acceptably for four minutes at 350°F (175°C) until warm through, and no longer than that.

title: Cheddar And Chive Biscuits
dek: Sharp cheddar cut in with the butter, salt dialled back, baked cooler so the cheese does not burn.
intro: Cheese is about a third fat and carries a fair amount of salt, so a cheddar biscuit made by adding cheese to a plain recipe comes out heavy and over-seasoned. Two adjustments fix it: less butter, because the cheese brings its own, and less salt for the same reason. Grate the cheese coarse and cut it in with the butter rather than folding it in at the end, so it is distributed as pieces that melt into pockets. Bake it at 425 rather than 450 — exposed cheese scorches and turns bitter well before a biscuit is done at the higher heat.

items: 140 g cold unsalted butter, cubed (about 10 tbsp)
170 g sharp cheddar, coarsely grated (about 1 3/4 cups)

method: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Whisk the flour, baking powder, soda and salt.
Cut in the cold butter until the pieces are hazelnut sized and irregular.
Toss through the grated cheddar and chives so every shred is coated in flour. Coated cheese stays where you put it; uncoated cheese clumps and runs out the side during the bake.

Add the buttermilk and stir with a fork until just combined. Fat to flour here is 1:3 before the cheese and closer to 1:2.1 once you count the cheese fat, which is why the butter is down from the house recipe.
Pat out to 2 cm on a floured counter, fold in thirds twice, then pat to 2.5 cm.
Cut with a floured cutter pressed straight down, and set them on parchment with the sides just touching. Pick off any cheese sitting on the outside — it will scorch and stick.
Brush with melted butter and grind pepper over the tops.
Bake 18 to 22 minutes, until well risen, deep gold, and the cheese that has leaked at the edges is browned and lacy rather than black. An instant-read reads 205°F (96°C).
Cool five minutes on the tray so the melted cheese sets and they lift off cleanly.
If they came out squat and greasy, the cheese was soft or finely grated. Use it cold and coarse.
notes: An aged cheddar gives more flavour per gram than a mild one, which means you use less of it and the dough stays light.
Spring onion greens work if there are no chives. Anything wetter than that — grated courgette, fresh tomato — will not.
storage: Two days in a tin. Split and toast them cut side down in a dry pan until the cheese sizzles again.

title: Sweet Potato Biscuits
dek: Roasted, not boiled, with the liquid held back because purée moisture is never the same twice.
intro: Roast the sweet potatoes; do not boil them. Boiling waterlogs the flesh and you spend the rest of the recipe compensating for liquid you added on purpose. Roasted purée is denser, sweeter and drier, and it still varies enough between one potato and the next that the buttermilk has to be held back and added by feel. These are soft rather than flaky, faintly sweet, and orange in a way that surprises people. They are the right thing under a slice of ham and they make an unreasonable amount of sense with chowder.

items: 2 medium sweet potatoes, about 700 g whole
300 g roasted flesh, cooled and mashed smooth (about 1 1/4 cups)
130 g cold unsalted butter, cubed (about 9 tbsp)
60 to 90 g cold buttermilk (about 1/4 to 1/3 cup)

method: Roast the sweet potatoes whole at 400°F (205°C) for 50 to 70 minutes, until a knife slides through with no resistance and the skins have wrinkled and started weeping caramel onto the tray. Cool completely, then scoop and mash. Warm purée melts the butter later.
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Whisk the flour, baking powder, soda, salt, sugar and spices together.
Cut in the butter to hazelnut-sized pieces.

Stir 60 g of the buttermilk into the cold purée to loosen it, then add that to the flour and stir with a fork. Add more buttermilk 15 g at a time only if there is dry flour left in the bowl. A dry-roasted potato might want the full 90 g and a wet one none at all.
Bring it together on a floured counter, pat to 2 cm, fold in thirds twice. This dough is softer and stickier than a plain biscuit dough and needs a lighter hand and more flour on the counter.
Pat to 2.5 cm and cut with a floured 2 3/4 inch cutter, straight down.

Set on parchment with sides touching and bake 18 to 22 minutes, until risen, dry to the touch, and browned at the edges — the tops stay orange and will not go golden the way a plain biscuit does, so use the edges as your guide. An instant-read reads 205°F (96°C).
Cool five minutes. They are fragile hot and firm up quickly.
If they are gummy in the middle, the purée was too wet. Next time spread it on a tray and dry it in a low oven for 15 minutes before using it.
notes: Tinned pumpkin works in place of the purée at the same weight and is more consistent, if less interesting.
A tablespoon of honey brushed on the hot tops with the butter turns these into something to eat on their own.
storage: Three days in a tin — the purée keeps them moist longer than a plain biscuit. They freeze well baked.

title: Biscuits Built For Gravy
dek: A leaner biscuit at 1:4 fat to flour that soaks without dissolving, and the sausage gravy to put on it.
yield: Eight biscuits and enough gravy for all of them
intro: A rich flaky biscuit is the wrong tool under gravy. All that butter makes fine layers and those layers slide apart and turn to paste the moment something wet lands on them. What you want here is leaner and tighter: fat to flour at one to four, which builds a sturdier crumb with a closer grain that absorbs gravy and still holds a fork. It is a worse biscuit on its own and a considerably better one under a ladle, which is the whole argument. The gravy is a plain roux gravy and the pepper is not optional.

items: 120 g cold unsalted butter, cubed (about 8 1/2 tbsp)
450 g breakfast sausage, casings removed (about 1 lb)
1 tsp cracked black pepper, and more after

method: Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C). Whisk the flour, baking powder, soda and salt.
Cut in the cold butter until it is mostly pea-sized with nothing larger than a hazelnut. Less butter than usual means it disperses faster, so check earlier than you would otherwise.
Add the buttermilk and stir with a fork until just together. At 73% hydration this dough is wetter than the house biscuit, which is deliberate: less fat, more water, a tighter and stronger crumb.
Pat out 2 cm thick, fold in thirds once only. One fold gives some structure without building the fragile layers you are trying to avoid here.
Pat to 2.5 cm, cut straight down with a floured cutter, and set them on a tray with sides touching.
Bake 15 to 18 minutes, until the tops are gold and the sides look dry and set rather than damp, and an instant-read reads 205°F (96°C).

While they bake, start the gravy. Break the sausage into a cold heavy skillet and put it over medium heat. Cook, breaking it up, until it is well browned in patches, no pink remains, and an instant-read in the thickest crumble reads 160°F (71°C).

Look at the fat in the pan. You want about 45 g of it. Pour off the excess or add butter to make up the difference, because the flour needs a matching weight of fat to make a roux that will not go greasy or grainy.
Scatter the flour over the meat and stir constantly for two minutes, until the raw flour smell is gone and the mixture looks like wet sand clinging to the sausage.
Add the milk in three lots, stirring hard after each and letting it thicken before the next. Adding it all at once is how you get lumps.

Simmer gently 6 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the gravy coats the back of a spoon and holds a line when you draw a finger through it. It will thicken further off the heat, so stop while it is still a shade looser than you want.
Season with black pepper, nutmeg and salt to taste. Split the biscuits, ladle over, and add more pepper than seems polite.
If the gravy goes stodgy waiting, loosen it with a splash of milk over low heat until it flows again. If it broke and looks greasy, there was too much fat for the flour.
notes: Sage-heavy sausage is the traditional choice and the one that tastes like breakfast. Hot sausage works and needs less pepper.
The gravy is better with a splash of the water the potatoes were cooked in, if there happen to be potatoes.
storage: Gravy keeps three days in the fridge and reheats with milk. The biscuits are a same-day proposition.

title: The Twisted Root
dek: The overnight cinnamon roll: enriched dough shaped at night, proofed cold, baked at six.
yield: Nine large rolls in a 9 x 13 inch pan
totalTime: About 14 hours, most of it in the fridge
intro: These are proofed overnight in the fridge, which is not a shortcut so much as a rearrangement: the fiddly rolling and cutting happens at a civilised hour, and the morning job is turning an oven on. Cold proofing also firms the butter in the filling so it stays put instead of running out into the pan, and it gives the dough enough time to develop some flavour of its own rather than tasting only of cinnamon and sugar. They come out roughly the size of a hubcap, which is the size a cinnamon roll should be.

items: 170 g unsalted butter, very soft (about 12 tbsp)
200 g dark brown sugar (about 1 cup packed)

method: Mix the flour, sugar, salt and yeast, keeping salt and yeast apart until they meet the liquid. Add the milk and eggs and mix to a rough dough.

Knead 8 minutes until smooth and elastic, then add the soft butter in three lots, kneading each in fully. It will go slippery and refuse to hold together, then come back. Finished dough should be glossy and pull into a thin windowpane.
Bulk in a covered bowl until doubled, 60 to 90 minutes in a warm kitchen. If your house is cold, this is where the schedule slips — give it the time rather than more yeast.
Beat the filling ingredients to a smooth spreadable paste. Very soft butter, not melted: melted butter runs out of the roll and pools under it, then burns.
Roll the dough on a floured counter into a rectangle about 40 by 50 cm and 5 mm thick. Spread the filling right to the edges on three sides, leaving a clean 2 cm strip along the far long edge.
Roll up from the long side toward the clean strip, firmly but not so tight that the middle telescopes out when it proofs. Pinch the seam shut and lay it seam down.
Cut nine rolls with a length of unflavoured dental floss or a very sharp knife — slide the floss under, cross the ends over the top and pull. A knife squashes the spiral and floss does not.
Set them cut side up in a buttered 9 x 13 inch pan with room between them, cover tightly, and refrigerate 8 to 14 hours.

In the morning, take the pan out and let it stand at room temperature 60 to 90 minutes, until the rolls have puffed, grown into each other, and a gentle poke leaves a dent that fills slowly. Cold rolls put straight in the oven will be dense in the middle.

Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Bake 28 to 34 minutes, until the tops are deep gold, the filling is bubbling at the edges, and an instant-read into the doughy centre of a middle roll reads 190°F (88°C). The centre roll is always the last to be done and it is the one to test.
Rest 10 minutes before icing, so the icing softens into the surface without disappearing entirely. Ice them warm, not hot, and not cold.
If the middles rose up and popped out like a chimney, the roll was too tight. If the filling ran out and welded them to the pan, the butter was melted or the pan was underbuttered.
notes: Cream cheese icing is the standard here. There is a recipe for it in this section and it makes about twice what one pan needs, which nobody has ever objected to.
The pan should be metal. Glass insulates and the bases come out pale and doughy.
storage: Two days covered at room temperature. Reheat individually for 20 seconds in a microwave, or eight minutes at 300°F (150°C) until warmed through.

title: Same-Day Cinnamon Rolls
dek: Two and a half hours start to finish, with the yeast doubled and the dough kept warm.
yield: Twelve rolls in a 9 x 13 inch pan
intro: Sometimes the decision to make cinnamon rolls is made at nine in the morning and there is no overnight to work with. This is that version: more yeast, warmer liquid, a slightly leaner dough that develops faster, and rolls cut a little smaller so they bake through in half an hour. They are not quite as good as the overnight ones — a fast dough tastes mostly of butter and sugar, where a slow one tastes of bread as well — but the difference is smaller than the two-hour gap suggests, and nobody has ever handed one back.

items: 250 g whole milk, warmed to about 35°C (about 1 cup)
140 g unsalted butter, very soft (about 10 tbsp)
170 g dark brown sugar (about 3/4 cup packed)

method: Warm the milk to about 35°C — comfortably warm on the inside of a wrist, not hot. Anything above about 50°C starts killing yeast, and the difference is not visible, only later and in the pan.
Mix flour, sugar, salt and yeast, add the milk and egg, and bring to a rough dough. Knead 8 minutes until smooth, then work in the soft butter in two lots until glossy.

Bulk somewhere genuinely warm, around 80 degrees Fahrenheit (27°C), for 45 to 55 minutes, until doubled and domed. An oven with the light on and a tray of hot water in the bottom is the reliable trick in a cold house.
Beat the filling to a smooth paste while it rises.
Roll the dough into a rectangle about 35 by 45 cm, spread the filling to the edges leaving one clean long strip, and roll up firmly toward the clean edge.
Cut twelve rolls with dental floss and set them cut side up in a buttered 9 x 13 inch metal pan.

Prove warm 35 to 45 minutes, until the rolls have swollen into each other and a light poke leaves a dent that fills back slowly. Under-proofed rolls bake up tight and bready, and this is the step people rush.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) and bake 26 to 32 minutes, until the tops are deep gold, the filling bubbles at the edges, and an instant-read in the middle roll reads 190°F (88°C).
Rest 10 minutes, then ice while warm.
If the crumb is coarse and yeasty-tasting, that is the cost of the fast schedule and 2.2% yeast. Dropping the yeast to 8 g and adding 40 minutes closes most of the gap.
notes: A hot kitchen makes this schedule shorter still. Judge by the dough, not the clock, particularly in summer.
The dough can be made in a stand mixer in 6 minutes on medium, which is worth doing here since speed is the point.
storage: Two days covered. Warm briefly before eating; cold cinnamon rolls are a different and lesser thing.

title: Cream Cheese Icing
dek: The icing for the cinnamon rolls, with the temperature rules that decide whether it melts in or sits on top.
yield: About 670 g, enough for two pans of rolls
intro: There are two icings, and which one you want depends on when you put it on. Applied to a roll straight from the oven it melts and soaks in and becomes part of the thing, sweet and glossy and invisible. Applied to a cold roll it sits on top in a thick pale layer and stays there. Both are legitimate and the recipe is the same; the only variable is the temperature of what is underneath. The mistake is doing it at the temperature in between, where it half-melts and slides off the sides into a puddle.

items: 225 g full-fat cream cheese, at cool room temperature (about 8 oz)

method: Get the temperatures right first. Both the butter and the cream cheese should be around 18°C — soft enough to dent under a finger, firm enough to hold a shape. An instant-read pushed into the middle of the block is the least argumentative way to know. Cold cream cheese gives you lumps that never beat out; warm cream cheese gives you a soup that no amount of sugar will thicken.
Beat the butter alone for a minute until it is pale and smooth. Doing the butter first is what stops the lumps.
Add the cream cheese and beat just until combined, 30 seconds or so. Cream cheese thins when it is over-beaten, because the emulsion breaks. This is the single most common way this icing is ruined.
Add the sifted icing sugar in two lots on low speed, then the sour cream, vanilla and salt. Beat 20 seconds more, no longer.

Check the consistency. It should fall off a spoon in a thick ribbon that holds for a second before flattening. Too stiff, add sour cream 10 g at a time. Too loose, chill it for 20 minutes rather than adding more sugar, which only makes it sweeter and stickier.

For icing that melts in: spread it on rolls that have rested 10 minutes out of the oven, still hot enough to steam. For icing that sits on top: wait until they are completely cool, and use it straight from the fridge.
The pinch of salt and the sour cream are both there to cut the sweetness. Leave them out and it tastes like frosting from a tub.
notes: Full-fat block cream cheese only. The spreadable kind in a tub has added water and gums and it will not set.
For a thinner glaze for scones or buns, use 100 g cream cheese, 200 g icing sugar and 40 g milk instead.
storage: Five days in the fridge in a sealed tub. Bring it back to about 18°C and beat it briefly before using, or it will tear the surface of whatever you spread it on.

title: Pecan Sticky Buns
dek: A caramel goo in the bottom of the pan, buns baked on top of it, and the whole thing inverted while hot.
yield: Twelve buns in a 9 x 13 inch pan
intro: A sticky bun is a cinnamon roll baked upside down on top of a caramel. The goo is butter, brown sugar and syrup, and it does two jobs: it caramelises into a sauce under the buns, and it steams up through them so the crumb stays wet. The critical part is inverting the pan while everything is still hot enough to flow. Leave it five minutes too long and the caramel sets into toffee, welds itself to the pan, and you will be chiselling pecans out of it while everyone watches.

items: 200 g dark brown sugar (about 1 cup packed)
120 g honey or golden syrup (about 1/3 cup)
80 g unsalted butter, very soft (about 6 tbsp)
120 g light brown sugar (about 1/2 cup packed)

method: Mix and knead the dough as for any enriched dough: everything but the butter first, 8 minutes to smooth, then the soft butter worked in until glossy and windowpaning. Bulk until doubled, 60 to 90 minutes warm.

Make the goo. Melt the butter with the brown sugar, honey, cream and salt over medium heat, stirring, until it is smooth, glossy, and just beginning to bubble at the edges — about three minutes. Do not boil it hard; you are making a sauce, not a candy, and boiling drives it toward toffee.
Pour the goo into a buttered 9 x 13 inch metal pan and scatter the pecans over it evenly, flat side down.
Beat the filling to a paste. Roll the dough to a 35 by 45 cm rectangle, spread the filling to the edges bar one clean strip, and roll up firmly.
Cut twelve buns with floss and set them cut side up on the goo, leaving space between them.

Prove 45 to 60 minutes at room temperature, until swollen and touching and a poke leaves a slow-filling dent. Or cover and refrigerate overnight, then bring back to room temperature for an hour in the morning.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Put the pan on a foil-lined tray, because the goo will boil over and burnt caramel on an oven floor is a genuinely unpleasant afternoon.

Bake 32 to 38 minutes, until the tops are deep brown, the caramel is bubbling thickly up the sides, and an instant-read in the centre bun reads 190°F (88°C). Underbaked sticky buns are gummy in the middle and the caramel never sets properly.

Rest exactly five minutes — long enough for the caramel to stop being molten, short enough that it still flows. Run a knife round the edge, put a tray over the pan, and invert the whole thing in one confident movement.
Leave the pan sitting on top for a minute so the last of the caramel runs down, then lift it off and scrape any stragglers back onto the buns.
If the caramel set hard in the pan, put it back in the oven for three minutes until it loosens, then invert again. If it ran thin and soaked away, the goo was boiled too long and lost water.
notes: Toasting the pecans first at 350°F (175°C) for 7 minutes, until fragrant, is worth the extra tray.
Golden syrup gives a cleaner caramel flavour than honey. Honey gives a floral note that some people like and some do not.
storage: Two days at room temperature under a cloth. Reheat for six minutes at 300°F (150°C) until the caramel loosens again.

title: Morning Buns
dek: A quick-laminated dough with three folds, cinnamon sugar and orange zest, baked in a muffin tin.
totalTime: About 6 hours, or overnight for the dough
intro: A morning bun is a croissant that got rolled in cinnamon sugar and baked in a muffin tin, which fixes the two hardest things about croissants: shaping, and the way a pastry that size goes stale by noon. The lamination is a simplified three-fold version — enough butter layers for a proper shatter, not so many that a home kitchen has to keep everything at pastry-room temperature for an afternoon. The muffin tin does real work: it traps the butter as it renders, so the outside fries and caramelises instead of leaking away.

items: 200 g whole milk, cold (about 3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp)
40 g caster sugar for rolling the hot buns (about 3 tbsp)

method: Mix the dough ingredients and knead 5 minutes to a smooth, firm dough. Do not over-develop it; a very strong dough fights the rolling later. Flatten to a rectangle, wrap, and refrigerate at least 2 hours or overnight.

Make the butter block. Beat the cold butter between two sheets of parchment with a rolling pin into a 15 by 15 cm square, then chill it 15 minutes. It should be pliable and cold — if it cracks it is too cold, if it shines it is too warm.
Roll the dough to 30 by 15 cm, lay the butter block over the bottom half, and fold the top down. Seal the edges by pressing with the pin.

Roll out to about 45 by 20 cm and give it a letter fold. Wrap and chill 30 minutes. Repeat twice more, for three folds total, chilling between each. If butter breaks through the surface at any point, patch it with a dusting of flour and get it back in the fridge.
Mix the filling sugar, cinnamon and orange zest, rubbing the zest through the sugar with your fingers until it smells strongly of orange.
Roll the dough out to about 30 by 45 cm and 5 mm thick. Scatter the filling evenly over the whole surface and press it lightly in with the pin so it does not all fall out when you roll.
Roll up from the long side into a tight log and cut twelve pieces. Set each cut side up in a well-buttered muffin tin, pressing down gently.

Prove at cool room temperature, around 21°C, for 90 minutes to 2 hours, until visibly puffed and jiggly and roughly half again as big. Warmer than that and the butter melts out before it ever gets to the oven, which is the classic way to lose a morning's work.

Heat the oven to 400°F (205°C). Bake 22 to 28 minutes, until the tops are deep brown and the sugar at the edges has caramelised to a dark lacquer. Pale morning buns are underbaked and doughy in the spiral.
Lift them out of the tin immediately with a fork — waiting means the caramel sets and they stay in — and roll the hot buns in the extra caster sugar.

Cool five minutes and eat them warm. If a pool of butter collected in each cup, the dough was proved too warm or the lamination broke down. It still tastes good and it is not the pastry you were aiming for.
notes: This lamination is a rough one on purpose. If you want proper croissant layering, do six folds and expect to spend a day on it.
Cardamom in place of half the cinnamon is a good change, and it goes better with the orange.
storage: Day one only, honestly. They are 60% air and butter and by tomorrow they are a biscuit.

title: Soft Dinner Rolls
dek: A dozen pull-apart rolls with a milk and butter dough, brushed with more butter on the way out.
yield: Twelve rolls in a 9 x 13 inch pan
intro: These are the rolls that go next to a pot of something, get pulled apart at the table, and disappear before anybody remembers to put them on a plate. The dough is enriched with milk, butter, egg and a little sugar, which gives a fine, soft, slightly sweet crumb that stays tender for two days. They are baked touching so the sides stay pale and pillowy and only the tops brown. Straightforward yeasted dough, no preferment, no overnight, and about the most reliable thing in this section.

items: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp milk, for the wash
30 g melted butter for after baking (about 2 tbsp)

method: Mix flour, sugar, salt and yeast, add milk and egg, and bring together. Knead 8 minutes until smooth, then work in the soft butter until the dough is glossy and stretches thin without tearing.
Bulk covered until doubled, 60 to 90 minutes in a warm room. The dough should hold a dent when poked rather than springing straight back.

Divide into twelve pieces of about 80 g. Shape each by flattening it, folding the edges to the centre, then rolling it under a cupped hand on an unfloured patch of counter until the surface is taut and smooth. Flour under your hand stops it gripping, and without grip you cannot build tension.
Set them in a buttered 9 x 13 inch pan in three rows of four, evenly spaced with small gaps.
Prove covered 45 to 60 minutes, until they have grown into each other, filled the pan, and a light poke leaves a shallow dent that fills slowly.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) and brush the tops gently with egg wash.
Bake 22 to 28 minutes, until the tops are deep golden brown, the rolls have risen into a single slab, and an instant-read into a middle roll reads 190°F (88°C).
Brush with melted butter the moment they come out and scatter flaky salt over. The steam softens the crust as they cool, which is the texture you want.

Cool 15 minutes in the pan before pulling them apart. If the middle rolls are doughy while the outer ones are done, the pan was crowded or the oven runs cool — check the centre one and bake to temperature, not to time.
notes: The dough shapes into hot dog buns, cloverleaf rolls or a plain loaf without changing anything but the tin.
Made a day ahead: shape, refrigerate overnight, and prove for two hours from cold in the morning.
storage: Three days in a sealed bag. Refresh at 300°F (150°C) for five minutes until warm and soft again.

title: Potato Rolls
dek: Riced russet and its cooking water in the dough, for rolls that stay soft for four days.
totalTime: 3 hours 30 minutes, plus cooling the potato
intro: Potato does three useful things in a dough. Its starch gelatinises during cooking and then holds water in a way raw flour starch cannot, so the crumb stays moist. It brings no gluten, which softens the structure. And the cooking water carries dissolved starch and a little potassium, which the yeast likes. The result keeps noticeably longer than a plain roll of the same enrichment, which is why potato rolls turn up wherever bread has to survive a day. Use a floury russet, not a waxy potato, and rice it rather than mashing it.

items: 200 g riced cooked potato, cooled (about 1 cup, lightly packed)
150 g of the potato cooking water, cooled to lukewarm (about 2/3 cup)
1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for the wash

method: Peel and chunk the potato and simmer in unsalted water until a knife goes through with no resistance and the edges are starting to break down, 15 to 20 minutes. Save 150 g of the cooking water.
Rice or press the potato through a sieve while hot, then spread it out and cool it to lukewarm. Riced potato is fluffy; mashed potato is gluey, and glue in a dough makes a dense roll.
Mix the flour, sugar, salt and yeast. Add the potato, the cooking water and the egg, and bring to a dough. It will feel tacky and soft. Resist adding flour.
Knead 8 to 10 minutes, then work in the butter. Potato dough never gets as smooth or as elastic as a straight wheat dough — a slightly slack, silky feel is the target rather than a tight windowpane.
Bulk covered until doubled, 75 to 90 minutes. It rises well because of the extra starch, and it can run past its peak faster than you expect.
Divide into twelve pieces of about 85 g and shape each into a taut ball. Set them on a parchment-lined tray, spaced for pull-apart rolls or well apart for individual buns.
Prove 45 to 60 minutes, until puffy and holding a slow-filling dent.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C), brush with egg wash, and bake 18 to 22 minutes, until deep gold and glossy and an instant-read reads 190°F (88°C).
Brush with melted butter as they come out and cool on a rack.
If the crumb is heavy and damp, there was too much potato or it was mashed rather than riced. Two hundred grams to five hundred of flour is about the ceiling.
notes: Left-over mashed potato works if it has no butter, milk or salt in it. If it does, reduce the dough butter and salt accordingly.
Flattened to 10 cm across before proving, these are the best hamburger buns in this collection, though a brioche bun holds a fattier patty better.
storage: Four days in a bag on the counter, which is a day or two longer than a plain enriched roll would last.

title: Brioche Burger Buns
dek: Twenty-five percent butter, an overnight chill, and a bun that holds together under a wet patty.
yield: Eight buns, about 110 g each baked
totalTime: About 16 hours, mostly overnight in the fridge
intro: These are brioche in ratio if not in ambition: butter at twenty-five percent of the flour weight, which is rich enough to give the close, tender, faintly yellow crumb people want and lean enough that the bun does not collapse under something hot and wet. The overnight chill is doing two jobs. It firms the butter so a very soft dough becomes shapeable, and it gives the flavour somewhere to develop, because a dough with this much sugar and fat ferments fast and tastes of very little if you rush it.

items: 200 g whole milk, cold (about 3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp)
1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp milk, for the wash

method: Mix the flour, sugar, salt and yeast, add the cold milk and eggs, and bring to a dough. Knead 10 minutes, until it is smooth and strong — build the gluten thoroughly before any butter goes near it, because fat coats the proteins and stops them linking.

Add the butter 25 g at a time, working each piece in completely before the next. The dough will break apart into a greasy mess after each addition and come back together within a minute. If it stays greasy, it is too warm; chill it for 15 minutes and carry on.
Knead until glossy, elastic and pulling cleanly from the bowl. It should stretch into a thin, even, translucent sheet.
Bulk one hour at room temperature, then cover and refrigerate 8 to 14 hours. Cold brioche dough handles like modelling clay; warm brioche dough handles like something you want to throw away.
Divide the cold dough into eight pieces of about 120 g and shape each into a tight ball on an unfloured counter.

Set them well apart on a parchment-lined tray and flatten each gently with your palm to about 9 cm across. Flattening now gives you a bun rather than a ball; brioche puffs up more than you think it will.

Prove 2 to 3 hours from cold, until nearly doubled, visibly domed, and a light poke leaves a dent that fills back slowly. Cold dough proves slowly and this stage always takes longer than people allow for.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush twice with egg wash, gently, and scatter sesame seeds.

Bake 16 to 20 minutes, until the tops are deep glossy brown and an instant-read in the centre of a bun reads 190°F (88°C). Enriched dough browns early because of the sugar and egg, so trust the thermometer over the colour.
Cool completely on a rack before splitting, at least an hour. Warm brioche compresses to nothing under a knife.
If the buns spread flat instead of doming, the shaping was slack or the dough was over-proofed. If the crumb is dense and the butter leaked out, it went in too fast or too warm.
notes: Toast the cut sides in a dry pan with a little butter before building anything on them. It is a seal against the juices as much as it is flavour.
The same dough at 60 g a piece makes slider buns, baked for 12 to 14 minutes to the same internal temperature.
storage: Three days in a bag. They freeze well split, which means you can toast them from frozen.

title: Spiced Currant Buns With Crosses
dek: Soaked currants, orange zest, a flour paste cross and a sugar glaze straight out of the oven.
intro: The spice mix matters more than the quantity of it: cinnamon on its own tastes flat here, and it wants allspice, nutmeg, clove and a little ginger behind it. Soak the dried fruit first, in tea or juice, or it will pull water out of the dough and bake into hard little stones. The crosses are a flour and water paste piped on before baking, which sets matte and pale, and the glaze goes on the second they come out so the heat drives it into the surface rather than leaving a sticky film.

items: 150 g hot strong tea or orange juice (about 2/3 cup)
50 g candied peel, chopped, optional (about 1/3 cup)
12 g mixed ground spice — 6 g cinnamon, 3 g allspice, 2 g nutmeg, 1 g clove (about 2 tsp total)
60 g caster sugar for the glaze (about 1/4 cup)
60 g water for the glaze (about 1/4 cup)

method: Pour the hot tea over the currants and raisins and leave them to soak at least an hour, until plump and the liquid is mostly taken up. Drain well and pat dry. Wet fruit slackens the dough and leaves grey streaks.
Mix the flour, sugar, salt, yeast and spices, add the milk and egg, and bring to a dough. Knead 8 minutes to smooth, then work in the butter until glossy.

Flatten the dough out, scatter the drained fruit, peel and orange zest over it, and fold and knead just until distributed, a minute at most. Over-working now tears the fruit into the dough and greys it.
Bulk covered until doubled, 75 to 90 minutes. Spice slows yeast slightly and fruit sugar speeds it up, and in practice they roughly cancel out.
Divide into twelve pieces of about 100 g and shape each into a tight ball. Set them in a buttered 9 x 13 inch pan in three rows of four, with small gaps.
Prove 45 to 60 minutes, until swollen, touching, and holding a slow-filling dent.

Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Whisk the cross paste flour and water to a smooth pipeable batter — thick enough to hold a line, loose enough to pipe — and pipe crosses over the buns from a bag with a small plain nozzle or a snipped corner.
Bake 20 to 25 minutes, until the buns are deep brown between the crosses, the crosses themselves are set and matte, and an instant-read in a middle bun reads 190°F (88°C).
While they bake, boil the glaze sugar and water together until the sugar has dissolved and the syrup just starts to thicken and coat a spoon, two to three minutes.
Brush the glaze over the buns the moment they leave the oven, twice, and let it dry to a shine on the hot surface.
Cool in the pan 15 minutes. If the crosses spread and vanished, the paste was too thin; if they cracked and lifted off, too thick.
notes: Chopped dried apricot or sour cherries in place of half the currants make a better bun and a less traditional one.
The spice mix keeps in a sealed tub, so mix ten times what you need and save yourself four jars next time.
storage: Two days in a tin. On day three they are better split and toasted with butter, which is arguably their best form anyway.

title: Sourdough Cinnamon Rolls
dek: Naturally leavened, bulked overnight, with enough tang to argue with the sugar.
yield: Nine rolls in a 9 x 13 inch pan
intro: The case for making these with a starter rather than yeast is not that it is more virtuous. It is that a cinnamon roll is an enormous amount of sugar and butter, and a little acidity underneath it stops the whole thing tasting like a dessert at eight in the morning. A naturally leavened enriched dough is slow — sugar and fat both hold yeast back, and wild yeast is not fast to begin with — so this runs overnight at room temperature and gets shaped in the morning, which is the opposite way round from the yeasted version.

items: 150 g unsalted butter, very soft (about 10 1/2 tbsp)
180 g dark brown sugar (about 3/4 cup packed)

method: Build the levain on milk in the morning and use it at peak, six to eight hours later, when it is domed and smells sour and sweet at once.
In the evening, mix flour, sugar, milk, eggs and levain to a rough dough and rest 30 minutes. Add the salt and knead 8 minutes to smooth.
Work in the soft butter in three lots. Enriched sourdough is slack and takes longer to come back together than a yeasted dough; keep going until it is glossy and stretches thin.

Bulk overnight at cool room temperature, around 20°C, for 10 to 14 hours. It should rise by about three-quarters and be soft and airy. In a warm house use the fridge for the second half of the night or it will be over the top by morning.
In the morning, beat the filling to a paste. Roll the dough on a floured counter to about 35 by 45 cm.
Spread the filling to the edges leaving one clean long strip, roll up firmly, and cut nine rolls with dental floss.

Set them cut side up in a buttered 9 x 13 inch metal pan and prove 2 to 4 hours at room temperature, until visibly swollen, touching, and holding a slow-filling dent. Sourdough enriched dough proves slowly and this is not a step to hurry — under-proofed rolls come out tight and heavy and taste sour rather than complex.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Bake 30 to 36 minutes, until deep gold, bubbling at the edges, and an instant-read in the middle roll reads 190°F (88°C).
Rest 10 minutes and ice while warm.
If they taste flatly sour instead of tangy, the levain was past peak or the bulk ran long in a warm room. If they are dense, the prove was short.
notes: Discard will not do this. It needs a levain at peak, and the dough needs the lift more than any lean bread does.
For a morning bake, shape at night and cold proof 10 to 12 hours, then give the pan two hours at room temperature before it goes in.
storage: Two days covered. Naturally leavened rolls stale slightly slower than yeasted ones, which is a small consolation for the extra day.

title: Plain Scones
dek: Low fat, high leavening, cut deep and straight, out of the oven in twelve minutes.
intro: A scone is not a sweet biscuit, whatever the shape suggests. The fat is far lower — about one part to five and a half here, against one to two point eight in the house biscuit — and the leavening is much higher, so the lift comes chemically rather than from steam in butter layers. That makes a lighter, cakier, more open crumb that is built to carry jam and cream. They also go stale within hours, which is not a flaw so much as a schedule: make them when people are already in the house.

items: 80 g cold unsalted butter, cubed (about 5 1/2 tbsp)
1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp milk, for the tops

method: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) and line a tray. Scones want a hot oven and a short bake; a slow one dries them out before they have finished rising.
Whisk the flour, baking powder, sugar and salt together properly. Twenty grams of baking powder is a lot and it has to be evenly distributed or you get bitter patches.
Rub in the cold butter with your fingertips until it looks like fine breadcrumbs. Unlike a biscuit, you want it evenly dispersed here — no visible pieces.

Beat the egg into the milk and add it all at once. Bring it together with a knife blade held flat, cutting through rather than stirring, until it just forms a soft dough. It should be softer and stickier than a biscuit dough.
Turn out onto a floured counter and pat, do not roll, to 3 cm thick. Thin scones do not rise; the height you cut is close to the height you get plus half again.
Dip a 2 inch cutter in flour and press straight down through the dough without twisting. Twisting seals and pinches the edge, and pinched scones come out lopsided every time.
Set them on the tray close together, about 2 cm apart, and brush the tops only with egg wash. Egg down the sides glues the rise shut.
Bake 10 to 14 minutes, until well risen, golden on top, and the sides show a pale band and a clear break line. Tapped underneath they should sound light and hollow.
Cool on a rack five minutes and eat them warm. If they came out flat, the likely reasons are dough patted too thin, a twisted cutter, or baking powder that has lost its fizz.
notes: For fruit scones, add 100 g sultanas soaked briefly in hot water and drained.
Buttermilk in place of the milk, with 4 g of the baking powder swapped for baking soda, gives a slightly tangier and more tender scone.
storage: Same day, and really the same hour. Day-old scones split and toasted are still worth eating; day-old scones as they are, are not.

title: Marionberry Cream Scones
dek: Frozen berries folded in hard and fast, a rich cream dough, cut in wedges and frozen before baking.
intro: Marionberries are wetter and softer than blueberries and they will happily turn a scone dough purple and slack if you let them. Two rules keep that from happening: use them frozen, straight from the freezer with no thawing, and fold them in with the fewest possible movements. This is the American style of scone, richer than the plain kind and closer to a biscuit in ratio at one part butter to two point eight parts flour, with cream doing the work of the milk. Freezing the cut wedges before baking keeps them tall.

items: 150 g cold unsalted butter, cubed (about 10 1/2 tbsp)

method: Whisk the flour, baking powder, sugar, salt and lemon zest together, rubbing the zest through the sugar first so it does not clump.
Cut in the cold butter until the largest pieces are pea-sized. Put the bowl in the freezer for 10 minutes while you get everything else ready.
Beat the egg into the cream. Pour it into the cold flour mixture and stir with a fork about eight times — it should still look dry and unpromising.

Tip the frozen berries in and fold four or five times with a scraper, no more. There will be dry patches. Bring it together on the counter with two or three presses and accept that it looks rough. Every additional movement crushes another berry.
Pat into a single round about 20 cm across and 3 cm thick. Cut into eight wedges with a floured knife, pressing straight down.

Space them on a parchment-lined tray and freeze the whole tray for 15 minutes. Meanwhile heat the oven to 400°F (205°C). Cold dough into a hot oven is what keeps the butter in pieces long enough to steam.
Brush the tops with cream and scatter demerara over.

Bake 22 to 26 minutes, until risen and deep golden at the edges, the berry juice is bubbling dark at the seams, and the bottoms are browned when you lift one. An instant-read in the centre of a wedge reads 205°F (96°C).
Cool 10 minutes on the tray before moving them, or the hot berry pockets tear straight through.
If the dough went lavender and sticky, the berries thawed. It will still bake, it will just be a berry cake rather than a scone.
notes: Blackberries, blueberries and chopped frozen strawberries all work. Fresh berries do not, unless you freeze them first on a tray.
Marionberry is a blackberry cross bred here in Oregon and it runs juicier than most, which is why the freezing rule matters more with these than with anything else.
storage: Best the day they are baked. Unbaked wedges freeze for a month and bake from frozen with five minutes added.

title: Shortcake For Berries
dek: A sweet biscuit that splits clean, built to sit under fruit and cream without going to mush.
intro: Sponge cake under strawberries is a compromise nobody asked for. Shortcake proper is a sweet biscuit: sturdy enough to hold up under macerated fruit and a pile of cream, tender enough not to fight the fork, and split horizontally so the juice soaks into the cut faces rather than sitting on top. Fat to flour is a shade under one to three, and the sugar is kept moderate because the fruit and cream bring plenty. Make them the same day, and macerate the fruit while they bake.

items: 140 g cold unsalted butter, cubed (about 10 tbsp)
200 g heavy cream, cold (about 3/4 cup plus 1 tbsp)
700 g strawberries or marionberries, hulled and sliced (about 5 cups)
50 g caster sugar for the fruit (about 1/4 cup)
300 g heavy cream for whipping (about 1 1/4 cups)

method: Heat the oven to 400°F (205°C). Whisk the flour, baking powder, sugar and salt.
Cut in the cold butter until the largest pieces are pea to hazelnut sized.

Beat the egg into the cream and stir it in with a fork until the dough just holds together. Total liquid runs at about 62% of the flour, firmer than a biscuit, because these have to stand up to wet fruit.
Pat out to 2 cm, fold in thirds once, then pat to 3 cm thick.

Cut eight rounds with a floured 3 inch cutter, straight down and no twist, and space them on a tray. Brush the tops with cream and scatter demerara over — the sugar crust is doing work here, both texture and a barrier against the juice.
Bake 18 to 22 minutes, until well risen, deep gold on top and browned underneath, and an instant-read reads 205°F (96°C).

While they bake, toss the fruit with the caster sugar and lemon juice and leave it at room temperature. It is ready when the sugar has dissolved and there is a pool of dark syrup in the bowl, 20 to 30 minutes.
Whip the cream with the icing sugar to soft peaks — it should hold a shape and still fold over at the tip. Stiff cream sits on top like a hat; soft cream settles into the fruit.
Split the shortcakes horizontally while still slightly warm. Spoon fruit and syrup over the bottom half, add cream, and set the top back on at an angle.
Assemble at the table, not in advance. Ten minutes after they are built, the bottom half is soup.
notes: Macerating longer than an hour breaks the fruit down into jam. Half an hour is the sweet spot for strawberries.
A splash of the berry syrup brushed onto the cut faces before the fruit goes on is a good idea if the shortcakes have cooled.
storage: The shortcakes keep a day in a tin and reheat well. Assembled shortcake keeps for about as long as it takes to carry it to a chair.

title: English Muffins
dek: An 80% dough griddled slowly in rings, split with a fork, full of nooks.
intro: The nooks come from two things and neither is magic. The dough is wet, at eighty percent hydration, so the bubbles it makes are large and irregular. And it is cooked slowly on a griddle rather than baked, so the inside stays open and slightly under-set where a hot oven would dry it into a crumb. Split them with a fork, never a knife: the fork tears along the existing holes and leaves the ragged surface that catches butter, and a knife cuts straight through them and gives you two smooth discs.

items: 260 g whole milk, lukewarm (about 1 cup plus 1 tbsp)
40 g fine semolina or cornmeal (about 1/4 cup)
10 g butter for the griddle (about 2 tsp)

method: Mix the flour, salt and yeast, add the milk, water and honey, and stir to a very wet, sticky dough. It is closer to a thick batter than a bread dough and it is meant to be.
Beat it with a wooden spoon or a mixer for four minutes, then work in the soft butter. Hydration is 80% on the flour, so do not try to knead this on a counter.
Bulk covered 90 minutes to 2 hours, with one fold in the bowl at the halfway mark, until doubled and full of bubbles.

Scatter semolina thickly over a tray. Scoop the dough into eight pieces of about 95 g with a wet scoop, drop each onto the semolina, and roll them over so they are coated all round. Flatten each gently to about 8 cm across.
Prove 45 to 60 minutes uncovered, until visibly puffed and wobbling when the tray is nudged.

Heat a heavy skillet or griddle over low heat with a smear of butter. Low is the whole trick — an instant-read laid on the surface should read around 150°C. Too hot and the outside is dark before the middle is cooked, which is the classic English muffin failure.

Cook them in rings if you want tidy sides, or free-form if you do not mind them irregular. Give them 7 to 9 minutes on the first side, until the underside is evenly pale gold and the sides look dry and set about a third of the way up.

Turn and cook another 7 to 9 minutes, until the second side matches and an instant-read through the side reads 200°F (93°C). If they are browning in under five minutes, the pan is too hot; take it off the heat for a minute and start again.
Cool completely on a rack before splitting. Warm muffins tear badly and lose their structure.
Split with a fork: press the tines in all the way round the equator, working around twice, then pull apart with your thumbs.
If the insides are gummy and raw, the pan was too hot. If they are dense with small even holes, the dough was too dry or under-proofed.
notes: The same dough made with 100 g of levain in place of the yeast and bulked overnight is better still, and takes a day.
Metal crumpet rings or clean tuna tins with the ends cut out both work, and both need buttering.
storage: Three days in a bag. They are made to be toasted, so day two is not a real loss.

title: Crumpets
dek: A 160% batter, bicarbonate at the end, and rings on a low griddle until the holes open and set.
intro: A crumpet is a batter, not a dough, and the holes are not incidental — they are the entire product. Yeast makes the bubbles during the rest, and a slug of bicarbonate stirred in at the very end makes a second wave of gas that pushes them up through a batter loose enough to let them travel. Cook them low. The top has to set while the bubbles are still opening, and every crumpet that comes out solid and heavy was cooked too fast, too thick, or without the bicarbonate.

items: 100 g warm whole milk (about 1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp)
20 g butter or oil for the rings and pan (about 1 1/2 tbsp)

method: Whisk the flour, yeast and sugar with the warm water and milk until completely smooth. It will be a loose batter, around 160% hydration, roughly the consistency of thick double cream.

Cover and leave in a warm place for 60 to 90 minutes, until the surface is a mass of bubbles, the batter has risen and started to fall back, and it smells strongly of yeast. That collapse is the signal, not a problem.
Dissolve the bicarbonate in the 30 g of warm water with the salt and stir it through the batter. It will loosen further and foam. Leave it 20 minutes.

Heat a heavy skillet over low heat and butter it along with the inside of the rings well. An instant-read on the pan surface should read about 150°C. This is lower than feels right and it is the difference between crumpets and pancakes.

Set the rings in the pan and pour in enough batter to come about 1.5 cm up the side — roughly 60 g each. Too deep and the middle never sets; too shallow and there is no depth for the holes to form in.

Cook 8 to 12 minutes without touching them. Holes should rise and open across the surface from the edges inward, and the top should go from wet and glossy to matte and dry. If no holes appear in the first four minutes, the batter is too thick — whisk another 20 g of water into the rest.

When the top is set and dry to a fingertip, lift the rings off with a cloth and turn the crumpets. Cook the second side only 2 to 3 minutes, until it is lightly coloured. That side is meant to be pale.
Check one: an instant-read through the side should read 200°F (93°C), and a crumpet torn in half should be full of open channels rather than damp and cakey.
Cool on a rack. Crumpets are always toasted before eating, even fresh ones, which is why the first cook is so gentle.
If they came out smooth on top with no holes, either the batter was too thick, the bicarbonate was old, or the pan was too hot and the surface sealed before the gas got up through it.
notes: Batter that has sat too long tastes sharply of alcohol. Use it within about three hours of the bicarbonate going in.
Butter the rings every time. Crumpet batter welds to bare metal.
storage: Four days in a bag, or freeze them. They are designed for toasting, so age matters less here than anywhere else in this section.

title: Yeast Doughnuts
dek: An enriched dough fried at 350°F (175°C), turned once, glazed while hot.
intro: Frying is a temperature problem with a dough attached. Too cool and the doughnut sits in the oil absorbing it, and comes out heavy and greasy. Too hot and the outside is dark before the middle has cooked, which is worse because it looks finished. Three hundred and fifty is the number, and it drops every time you put dough in, so you fry in small batches and let it recover between them. A thermometer clipped to the pan is not optional here — this is the one recipe in this section where guessing has a real cost.

items: 2 litres neutral oil — canola, sunflower or peanut (about 8 cups)

method: Mix the flour, sugar, salt and yeast, add milk and eggs, and knead 8 minutes to a smooth dough. Work in the soft butter until glossy and elastic.
Bulk covered until doubled, 60 to 90 minutes. Or refrigerate overnight, which makes the dough much easier to cut and gives a better flavour.
Roll out on a floured counter to 1.5 cm thick — no thinner, or they fry through before they puff. Cut with a 3 inch cutter and a 1 inch cutter for the middles.
Set each on its own small square of parchment on a tray. The parchment lets you lower a proofed doughnut into the oil without deflating it, and then floats free.

Prove 45 to 60 minutes, until visibly puffed and light, and a very gentle poke leaves a dent that fills slowly. Over-proofed doughnuts collapse in the oil; under-proofed ones stay dense and do not get the pale ring around the middle.
Heat the oil in a heavy deep pan to 350°F (175°C), with a thermometer clipped to the side. Fill the pan no more than half way.

Fry two or three at a time, parchment side down, peeling the paper off with tongs after a few seconds. Fry 60 to 90 seconds, until the underside is an even deep gold and a pale band has formed around the middle where the dough sat above the oil.

Turn once and fry another 60 to 90 seconds, until the second side matches. Check the first one of each batch: an instant-read into the side should read 190°F (88°C). Turning them more than once makes them absorb oil.
Lift onto a rack over a tray, never onto paper towel, which traps steam against the base and turns it soggy.
Let the oil come back up to 350°F (175°C) between batches. It will have dropped 15 to 20 degrees Fahrenheit and frying at that lower temperature is exactly how greasy doughnuts happen.
Whisk the glaze ingredients smooth. Dip each doughnut while still warm, top side down, lift, twist, and set back on the rack to drip and set.
Eat them within a couple of hours. A doughnut is at its best somewhere around the fifteen minute mark and it is genuinely not the same thing by tomorrow.
notes: The holes fry in about 45 seconds a side and are the cook's payment.
Used frying oil, cooled and strained through a coffee filter, is good for one or two more rounds. Discard it once it smells sharp or foams.
storage: Same day only, and preferably within the hour. There is no honest way around this.
